guide.summary: Google Calendar access is set up through a Google Cloud project: you configure an OAuth consent screen under Google Auth platform > Branding, then create a client under Clients. An app for users outside your own Workspace organization must be External, list its scopes, and needs a verified-domain homepage and a hosted privacy policy. Restricted scopes also need an annual security assessment. Until the app leaves Testing status, only listed test users can connect, and their refresh tokens expire in 7 days. How long Google's review takes is not documented in the claims.
auth_alternatives: Service accounts: Google recommends these for server-to-server work, and no OAuth client ID is required. Choose this only when the agent acts as itself rather than on behalf of individual end users.

Internal (Workspace-only) app: if every user is inside your own Workspace organization, an Internal app needs no Google review even with sensitive or restricted scopes. The trade-off is that nobody outside the organization can connect.

reasons_to_bring_own: No Composio toolkit or managed auth information was provided for Google Calendar, so a borrowed app cannot be confirmed.
External apps outside Testing need your own consent screen branding, a verified-domain homepage and a privacy policy hosted on that domain, all tied to your project.
Refresh tokens for external apps in Testing expire in 7 days, so long-running agent access for real users requires your own published app.
build_or_borrow.verdict: Plan to build your own Google Cloud OAuth app, because no Composio managed auth was confirmed for Google Calendar and a published External app is the only documented way to give real users lasting access (use service accounts instead if the agent only needs server-to-server access, as Google recommends).

prerequisites.text: A Google account with access to the Google Cloud console. The console sits behind a login wall.
Agree to the Google API Services User Data Policy before creating the consent screen configuration. Google user data may not be sold to data brokers or used for ads.
A homepage on a verified domain that is not only a login page.
A privacy policy hosted on the homepage domain and linked from the consent screen.
An app name, a user support email, and a contact email for project change notifications.
If you use restricted scopes, an annual security assessment by a Google-empanelled assessor.

oauth.token_lifetime: Refresh tokens for External apps in Testing expire in 7 days. Any refresh token stops working if unused for six months. Access token lifetime is not documented in the claims.

blockers.text: An insufficient scope justification can get the app rejected.
blockers.workaround: Request the narrowest Calendar scopes you need and write a concrete justification for each one tied to a visible feature.

blockers.text: The homepage cannot be only a login page and must be on a verified domain.
blockers.workaround: Publish a real public landing page on a domain you control and verify it before submitting.

blockers.text: Restricted scopes require an annual security assessment by Google-empanelled assessors.
blockers.workaround: Avoid restricted scopes if you can. If you cannot, budget for a recurring assessment. Cost and duration are not documented in the claims.

blockers.text: The AI-agent client option cannot be changed after the client is created.
blockers.workaround: Decide on this setting before you click Create. If you get it wrong, create a new client.

app_specific_gotchas.text: While an External app is in Testing status, refresh tokens expire after 7 days, so test users must reconnect weekly.
Each account can hold only 100 refresh tokens per client ID. Issuing more silently invalidates the oldest one.
Refresh tokens stop working if unused for six months, so dormant agent users must reauthorize.
Once a consent screen is configured, it cannot be removed.
Web application clients do not use a client secret, so you save only the client ID.

paths.verdict: Easiest path. Users must all be in your own Workspace organization. No Google review is needed, even with sensitive or restricted scopes, so this can be done in one sitting. The consent screen cannot be removed once configured, and the AI-agent client option cannot be changed after the client is created, so decide both up front.

steps.title: Decide Internal vs External user type
steps.detail_md:
This is a developer decision that changes who can use the app. The agent can only lay out the trade-off.

- **Internal** (your Workspace organization only): no Google review, even with sensitive or restricted scopes (c22). Scopes only need to be listed for apps used outside your organization (c21).
- **External** (anyone outside your org, which a shareable agent integration needs): you must set User type to External and add scopes (c26). That leads to review and possibly a security assessment (later steps).

The consent screen cannot be removed once configured (c19), so settle this first.

Service accounts are Google's recommendation for server-to-server work and need no OAuth client ID (c33). They do not fit users connecting their own calendars.

steps.title: Draft consent screen copy and scope justifications
steps.detail_md:
The agent drafts everything the consent screen form asks for:

- App name (c15)
- User support email (c16)
- Developer contact email for notifications about project changes (c17)

It also writes a specific justification for each scope. An insufficient justification can cause rejection (c10).

The drafted data-use language must state that Google user data is not sold to data brokers or used for ads (c13).

The exact Calendar scope names are **not covered** by the provided claims. Pick them from Google's documentation; do not guess.

steps.title: Publish homepage and privacy policy on a verified domain
steps.detail_md:
Two requirements:

- The homepage must be on a verified domain and cannot be only a login page (c12).
- The privacy policy must be hosted on the homepage's domain and linked from the consent screen (c9).

The agent can draft page content. Domain verification (DNS) and publishing are developer tasks.

The domain verification procedure itself is not described in the provided claims.

steps.title: Sign in to the Google API Console and configure Branding
steps.detail_md:
1. Sign in to the console. A probe confirmed it sits behind a Google login wall (c41).
2. Go to Google Auth platform > Branding (c14).
3. Enter the app name, support email and contact email drafted in step 2 (c15, c16, c17).
4. Link the privacy policy (c9).
5. Agree to the Google API Services User Data Policy, which is required before the configuration is created (c18).

This cannot be undone: the consent screen cannot be removed once configured (c19).

steps.title: Set Audience to External, add test users and scopes
steps.detail_md:
1. Under Audience, set User type to External and add your scopes (c26, c21).
2. Add test users. External apps need them listed under Audience (c20).

While the app is in Testing status, refresh tokens issued to external apps expire in 7 days (c34). Expect testers to reconnect weekly.

steps.title: Create the OAuth client (decide the AI-agent option first)
steps.detail_md:
Go to Google Auth platform > Clients and choose Create Client (c23).

**Decide before creating:** the AI-agent client option is immutable after the client is created (c24). This is the developer's call. If unsure, the agent can lay out the trade-off, but it cannot be changed later.

Per the provided claim, client secrets are not used for Web application clients, so only the client ID is saved (c25). Store it in your secrets manager.

The agent can list your app's callback URLs to paste in. The redirect URI field itself is not documented in the provided claims.

steps.title: Write the integration code and token handling
steps.detail_md:
Probes found no OAuth or OpenID discovery document on calendar.google.com (c42, c43). Do not try to auto-discover endpoints from that host. The authorization and token endpoint URLs are **not covered** by the provided claims; take them from Google's documentation.

Token handling to build in:

- Refresh tokens stop working if unused for six months (c35). Detect this and prompt the user to reconnect.
- Each account can hold at most 100 refresh tokens per client ID; beyond that the oldest is invalidated (c36). Reuse a user's existing token instead of re-consenting on every connect.
- In Testing status, refresh tokens expire in 7 days (c34).

No Composio managed toolkit was found, so plan to own this code.

steps.title: End-to-end test with test users
steps.detail_md:
1. Connect each test user added in step 5 (c20).
2. Verify calendar reads and writes for the scopes you chose.
3. Confirm your reconnect path works when the 7-day Testing refresh token expires (c34).

steps.title: Submit for Google verification
steps.detail_md:
Submit the External app for review, using the scope justifications from step 2. Weak justifications are a stated rejection cause (c10).

Check before submitting:

- The homepage is not just a login page and is on a verified domain (c12).
- The privacy policy is on the same domain and linked from the consent screen (c9).

If you use restricted scopes, you also need an annual security assessment by Google-empanelled assessors (c11). Who you contract with and what it costs are not documented in the provided claims.

steps.title: Wait for Google review (and security assessment if restricted scopes)
steps.detail_md:
Google owns this time. **How long review takes is not documented** in the provided claims. The 0 in the estimate field means "unknown", not "zero time".

If you use restricted scopes, the security assessment (c11) adds further time. Its duration is also not documented, and the assessment recurs annually.

Internal-only apps skip this step entirely (c22).

steps.title: Handle rejection feedback if any
steps.detail_md:
If Google rejects the app, the documented causes to check first are:

- Insufficient scope justification (c10)
- Homepage or domain problems (c12)
- Privacy policy placement (c9)

The agent can redraft justifications and page copy. Resubmitting is a developer action.

steps.title: Move out of Testing and ship
steps.detail_md:
Once approved, move the app out of Testing status so users stop hitting the 7-day refresh token expiry (c34).

The exact console control for changing publishing status is not described in the provided claims.

After launch, keep the annual security assessment on the calendar if you use restricted scopes (c11). Keep honoring the data-use policy (c13).

belief_diff.topic: Does letting arbitrary users connect require provider review or verification?
belief_diff.prior_belief: Yes, Google requires OAuth app verification before arbitrary users outside the test list can connect, once the app requests sensitive or restricted scopes like Google Calendar.
belief_diff.finding: The claims imply review applies to external apps with scopes, since internal-only apps skip Google review even with sensitive or restricted scopes and external apps must change User type and add scopes, but no claim states that verification gates arbitrary users outside the test list.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Google's OAuth verification typically takes about 3 to 5 business days, though restricted-scope reviews can run 4 to 6 weeks.
belief_diff.finding: The claims do not mention review turnaround times.

belief_diff.topic: Limits while the app is unapproved
belief_diff.prior_belief: While unverified, the app is capped at 100 users total and shows an unverified-app warning screen to every user.
belief_diff.finding: The claims do not mention a 100-user cap or an unverified-app warning screen; the only 100-related claim concerns refresh tokens per account per client ID, which is a different limit.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Google charges no fee for OAuth verification, but restricted-scope apps may need an annual third-party security assessment that costs roughly 500 to 4500 dollars.
belief_diff.finding: The claims confirm that restricted scopes require an annual security assessment by Google-empanelled assessors, but do not state any fee amount or whether verification itself is free.

belief_diff.topic: Key prerequisites (domain, privacy policy, video, business verification)
belief_diff.prior_belief: Verification requires a verified owned domain on the authorized domains list, a public privacy policy URL, a demo video showing scope usage, and a homepage link, and business verification is not generally required for individuals.
belief_diff.finding: The claims say the privacy policy must be hosted on the app's homepage domain and linked from the consent screen, and the homepage must be on a verified domain and cannot be only a login page; they do not address the demo video or business verification.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Redirect URIs must be exact matches registered in the console, must use HTTPS except for localhost, and may not contain wildcards or unregistered domains.
belief_diff.finding: None of the claims address redirect URI rules.
